title: Printing Output
summary: Print text to the console with console.log, use escape sequences, and print several values on one line.
intro: Every program talks to you through its output. In JavaScript that starts with `console.log()`.

steps.title: Printing text with console.log
steps.body:
`console.log()` writes a line to the console. Put the text inside quotes: double quotes and single quotes both make a string, and this course uses double quotes.

```javascript
console.log("Hello");
console.log('World');
```

Every call ends its own line, so the next `console.log()` starts on a new one. Lines run top to bottom, in order.

A semicolon ends each statement. JavaScript can often guess where one belongs, but writing it yourself avoids surprises.

Anything after `//` on a line is a comment. JavaScript skips it, so use comments to leave notes for people reading the code.

```javascript
// This line is ignored
console.log("Shown"); // so is this part
```

example.title: Welcome banner
example.prompt: Print a three line welcome banner.
example.output:
Welcome to Hack University
Lesson 1: Printing Output
Let's write some code!
example.explanation: The comment is skipped. Each `console.log()` call writes its text and then moves to a new line, so three calls make three lines in the order they run. The apostrophe in `Let's` is fine because the string uses double quotes.

practice.title: Course card
practice.prompt:
Print a three line card for a course.

1. Print `Course: Algorithms`
2. Print `Level: Beginner`
3. Print `Status: Enrolled`

Expected output:

```text
Course: Algorithms
Level: Beginner
Status: Enrolled
```

steps.title: Escape sequences and blank lines
steps.body:
Some characters are hard or impossible to type straight into a string. A backslash starts an *escape sequence* that stands for one of them:

| Write | Prints |
| --- | --- |
| `\n` | a new line |
| `\"` | a double quote |
| `\'` | a single quote |
| `\\` | one backslash |
| `\t` | a tab |

```javascript
console.log("Line one\nLine two");
console.log("Say \"yes\"");
console.log('It\'s here');
```

`\n` lets one string print several lines. Escape a quote only when it matches the quotes around the string: inside double quotes an apostrophe needs no backslash.

The classic gotcha is the backslash itself. In `"C:\new"` the `\n` becomes a line break, and in `"C:\Temp"` the unknown `\T` silently drops its backslash and prints `C:Temp`. Write `"C:\\new"` to get one real backslash.

`console.log()` with nothing inside prints an empty line, handy for spacing output.

example.title: Address card
example.prompt: Print a two line address from one string, an empty line, a file path, and a quote.
example.output:
Hack University
42 Main Street

Saved to C:\Temp
She said "hi"
example.explanation: `\n` splits the first string across two lines. The empty `console.log()` adds a blank line. `\\` prints a single backslash, and `\"` puts double quotes inside a double-quoted string without ending it.

practice.title: Shipping label
practice.prompt:
Print a shipping label, a blank line, a path, and a status message.

1. Print `Ada Lovelace` and `12 Engine Lane` on two lines using one `console.log()` call with `\n`.
2. Print an empty line.
3. Print `C:\Users\ada` with escaped backslashes.
4. Print `It's "done"` with escaped double quotes.

Expected output:

```text
Ada Lovelace
12 Engine Lane

C:\Users\ada
It's "done"
```

steps.title: Printing several values at once
steps.body:
`console.log()` accepts several values separated by commas. Each value you pass is called an *argument*. It prints them on one line with a single space between each.

```javascript
console.log("Score", 90, "of", 100); // Score 90 of 100
```

Numbers are written without quotes and print as numbers. `true` and `false` are values too, and they print as words. Strings print without their quotes.

Three gotchas. The space comes for free, so `console.log("Score:", 90)` already prints `Score: 90`, and adding a space inside the string gives two. Number literals print in their shortest form, so `1.50` prints as `1.5`. Keep `%` followed by a letter, such as `%d`, out of the first string when you pass several values: Node reads it as a placeholder.

A comment between `/*` and `*/` can span several lines:

```javascript
/* Game status
   printed below */
console.log("Ready", true);
```

example.title: Game status
example.prompt: Print three status lines, each built from comma-separated values.
example.explanation: The block comment is skipped. Each call joins its values with single spaces: strings without their quotes, `3` and `250` as numbers, and `true` as a word.

practice.title: Scoreboard
practice.prompt:
Print a three line scoreboard, passing several comma-separated values to each call.

1. Print `Player Ada` from the strings `"Player"` and `"Ada"`.
2. Print `Score 1200` from the string `"Score"` and the number `1200`.
3. Print `Winner: false` from the string `"Winner:"` and the value `false`.

Expected output:

```text
Player Ada
Score 1200
Winner: false
```
hints: Write `1200` and `false` without quotes. The space between values is added for you.

recap:
- `console.log("text");` prints one line. Each call ends its own line.
- Strings go in double or single quotes. A semicolon ends each statement.
- `//` starts a line comment and `/* ... */` wraps a block comment.
- `\n` is a new line, `\"` and `\'` are quotes, `\\` is one backslash, `\t` is a tab.
- `console.log()` with no arguments prints an empty line.
- `console.log(a, b, c)` prints its values separated by single spaces. Numbers and `true` or `false` print without quotes.
